section.sectionSummaryBrief: Since Kesser is above the chain of descent, the avodah that draws it must be above the soul's faculties, in the mode of "with all your might," whereas avodah within Torah's limits draws only a light related to the world.
section.t: Now, since the aspect of Kesser
(the Supreme King)
is above the chain of descent,
therefore the avodah in man that draws down this aspect
must also be above the chain of descent of his faculties,
in the aspect of "with all your might."
For through the avodah of Torah and mitzvos as it is in a manner of measure and limitation
(the chain of descent within man),
only the light that is in the aspect of the chain of descent is drawn down.
And even though through the avodah of Torah and mitzvos
(even when the avodah is in measure and limitation)
a light more sublime than the aspect of the Garden of Eden is drawn down,
as is proven from what is said,
"And He placed him in the Garden of Eden to work it and to guard it,"
"to work it" refers to the 248 positive commandments, and "to guard it" refers to the 365 negative commandments,
meaning that the Garden of Eden for Adam was not a matter of receiving reward, but rather the Garden of Eden was the place of his avodah,
and through his avodah in the Garden of Eden he drew down lights more sublime than the aspect of the Garden of Eden,
nevertheless,
what is drawn down through avodah as it is in measure according to Torah is only that which pertains to the world,
and it is that through which the Torah sustains the world,
as it is stated in the Gemara,
"If Israel accept the Torah, you will endure."
But the drawing down of the light that is above the chain of descent is specifically through the avodah of "with all your might."

section.sectionSummaryBrief: Based on this, the superiority of Tu B'Av over Tu B'Nissan and Tu B'Tishrei is analogous to the superiority of "a king is served in the field" over the field itself, as the latter represents only worldly perfection while the former draws a light above the chain of descent.
section.t: According to the above, we can understand why the maamar first explains the interpretation of "a king is served in the field" to clarify the superiority of Tu B'Av over Tu B'Nissan and Tu B'Tishrei,
for the superiority of Tu B'Av over Tu B'Nissan and Tu B'Tishrei is analogous to the superiority of "a king is served in the field" over the aspect of the field as it is in itself.
For the superiority of the Garden of Eden
(the field)
which is the aspect of "the advantage of the land,"
meaning that the world is in a state of perfection
(as above),
is analogous to the moon being established in its fullness.
However,
this perfection is only the perfection of the world,
and even what is added in the Garden of Eden through the avodah of "to work it and to guard it"
(as it is in the measure of Torah)
is only that which pertains to the world,
and the same applies regarding the perfection of the moon on Tu B'Nissan and Tu B'Tishrei,
which is from the aspect of Torah.
But the perfection of the moon on Tu B'Av,
since it comes after the descent of Tisha B'Av, which descent arouses the avodah of "with all your might"
(as will be explained later),
is analogous to "a king is served in the field,"
a light that is above the chain of descent.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: Attaining the avodah of "with all your might" comes through contemplating the world's limitations and constraints, which arouses one to transcend them, and this explains the Zohar's second interpretation of "a king is served in the field" as a negative aspect that ultimately leads to the positive.
section.t: Now, in order to arrive at the avodah of "with all your might," which is above measure and limitation,
it is through contemplation of the constraints and limitations of the world.
For by feeling the constraints and limitations of the world,
this itself arouses him to go out from the constraints and limitations,
so that his avodah will be above measure and limitation.
And the more he feels the constraints and limitations,
in addition to the constraints and limitations of the world in general, there are also things that hinder and confuse avodas Hashem,
such as hunger and illness
[for when a person is hungry or ill, he cannot understand and contemplate, etc., and cannot serve Hashem
(meaning
that in order to serve Hashem when he is ill, he needs special effort)],
and all the more so the concealments and veils of the time of exile,
the more he feels the constraints and limitations,
this brings him more to the avodah of "with all your might,"
the departure from constraint and limitation.
And with this we can understand why the above discourse brings the second interpretation in the Zohar,
that "a king is served in the field" is for the worse,
that "field" is the aspect of the field of the Other Side
("in the field she found him"),
and "a king is served in the field" is that the Sefirah of Malchus, "her feet descend," etc., and becomes concealed in the field of the Other Side,
for contemplating the matter of "a king is served in the field" as it is for the worse,
which is the matter of the exile of the Shechinah
[the reason that the Shechinah is in exile is the exile of Israel,
that we were exiled because of our sins],
this contemplation arouses him so that his avodah will be above measure and limitation,
and through this a light above the chain of descent is drawn down,
"a king is served in the field" for the better.
